name: HOUSE OF 1000 PORK-SES BURGER (Topped with ham and bacon)

recipe.history:
The pig has occupied a unique position in the human food chain for ten thousand years, since its domestication from the Eurasian wild boar somewhere in the Near East and independently in China. No other animal converts scraps and waste into dense, flavorful protein as efficiently, and no other animal has inspired as many distinct preservation and preparation traditions across as many cultures. Ham — the cured and often smoked hind leg of a pig — is one of civilization's great inventions: a technology of salt, time, and sometimes smoke that transforms perishable meat into something that can last months or years while developing flavors of extraordinary complexity. The hams of Parma, the Ibérico de Bellota of Spain's dehesa pastures, the Smithfield hams of Virginia, the Black Forest hams of southern Germany, the York hams of northern England — each represents a distinct microbial ecosystem, a specific breed and diet and curing tradition that produces flavors as specific and terroir-driven as any wine. Bacon, meanwhile — the cured and smoked belly — is perhaps the most universally beloved of all pork preparations, its combination of fat and lean, smoke and salt, crispability and chewiness placing it in a category of its own in the hierarchy of breakfast and sandwich meats.

Ham and bacon on a single burger is an American idea in its purest form: the audacious doubling-down, the insistence on more. The bacon cheeseburger became a fixture of American drive-ins and diners in the 1950s and 1960s, when the combination of the crisp, salty, smoky strip with the fat-rich patty and melted cheese established itself as a template that has never been improved upon, only elaborated. Adding ham to that template — thick-sliced, glazed, slightly caramelized around the edges — introduces a different register of pork flavor: sweeter, more delicate, with a different texture than bacon. The two together on a single patty are not redundant; they are complementary, the way that a chord is not redundant for containing more than one note. Ham brings sweetness and tender bite; bacon brings smoke and crunch and rendered fat.

I remember the first time I put both ham and bacon on a single burger without irony or apology. I was feeding a group of people who all had strong opinions about which was better, and I settled the argument by using both. The result was unanimously and immediately approved, which is the kind of unanimous approval that rarely happens in a room full of people with strong opinions. What struck me most was that each element retained its identity — the ham still tasted like ham, the bacon still tasted like bacon — but together they created something more complex than either could produce alone. The smoked, rendered fat from the bacon seasoned the ham; the delicate sweetness of the ham moderated the intensity of the bacon. The beef patty between the two layers of pork was a bridge between two very different worlds of flavor, and it needed to be exactly right to carry the weight.

Two preparations of pork, both intense in their own ways, demand a patty that is cooked to the temperature that preserves its capacity to contribute rather than simply exist. A medium rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit brings its own dimension to the pork two ways — the iron-rich meatiness of beef, the fat that renders differently than either ham fat or bacon fat, the juice that soaks into the bun and mingles with the rendered bacon grease. A well-done patty adds nothing to this conversation; it merely provides a grey, dry surface for the pork to sit on. The medium rare patty is what transforms a pork-topped beef patty into a unified composition rather than a collection of assembled ingredients.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
4 thick slices (about 1/2 inch each) good quality smoked ham (such as Black Forest or Virginia ham)
instructions: 1. Make the maple-pepper bacon: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Arrange bacon strips on a wire rack set over a rimmed baking sheet. Mix maple syrup, black pepper, and cayenne and brush over both sides of the bacon. Bake 18–20 minutes until crisp and caramelized. Transfer to paper towels. Reserve rendered bacon fat.

2. Make the glazed ham: Melt butter in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add ham slices and cook 2 minutes per side until golden at the edges. Add brown sugar, Dijon mustard, apple cider vinegar, cloves, and pepper to the pan. Swirl and baste the ham for 1–2 minutes until the glaze is thick and sticky and the ham is caramelized. Remove from heat and keep warm.

3. Make the burger sauce: Whisk together mayonnaise, yellow mustard, ketchup, sweet relish, apple cider vinegar, onion powder, garlic powder, salt, and pepper until smooth and combined. Refrigerate until ready to use.

4. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
5. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
6. Divide into 4 equal portions. Shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 45 minutes.
7. Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions of about 170g each. Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
9. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Brush the skillet lightly with reserved bacon fat. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
10. Lay a slice of sharp cheddar on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam 30–45 seconds until cheese is melted.
11. Transfer patties to a resting rack and rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
12. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

13. Assemble: Spread burger sauce generously on both cut surfaces of each bun. Place iceberg lettuce and tomato slices on the bottom bun. Set the cheesed patty on top. Lay one slice of glazed ham on the patty, folding it to fit. Lay 2 strips of maple-pepper bacon across the ham. Add a few thin red onion rings. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately.
